L72.p: Among a group of animals, the youngest one defeats an enemy or adversary.

L101.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Benedict II 336.

L103.p: The unpromising hero is given great magical powers by a god or other supernatural being, which lets him succeed.

L110.p: A heading listing the various kinds of unpromising heroes and heroines, so the types can be looked up under it.

L111.p: A hero or heroine who comes from humble, unpromising beginnings and nonetheless rises to greatness.

L111.1.r: **A. Nutt FLR IV 1ff.; *Hibbard 111 n. 6; Boccaccio Decameron II No. 8 (Lee 39); v. Hahn Sagenwissenschaftliche Studien 341ff.; *Dickson 42 n. 42; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
L111.1.p: A hero who is sent away or banished as a child, then comes back later and succeeds, often triumphing over those who cast him out.

L111.1.1.p: A young person who is banished grows up to become a powerful king.

L111.1.2.p: A bull-calf that runs away returns when full grown and defeats his own father.

L111.2.r: *Dickson 144ff. n. 147; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 120b; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri-French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Tonga: Gifford 130; N. A. Indian: Lowie JAFL XXI 27.

L111.2.2.p: A future hero is found as a baby lying on the shore.

L111.2.4.p: A future hero is found as a baby in a wolf's den and survives there.

L111.6.p: A hero who is the son of a hermit or religious recluse.

L111.7.p: A future hero or heroine who is raised by an animal after being left alone as a child.

L111.9.p: The hero of the story is a neglected grandson of a raja (an Indian king or prince), overlooked by his family at first.

L111.10.p: The fourth son, who seems the least promising of the brothers, is the one who ends up succeeding to the throne or inheritance.

L112.p: The hero or heroine is unattractive or physically unimpressive in appearance, yet still turns out to be the one who succeeds.

L112.1.p: The hero is itself a monster, such as a giant or beast-like creature, who nonetheless performs heroic deeds.

L112.8.p: The hero is a lame child, someone who cannot walk properly, yet becomes the central figure of the tale.

L112.9.p: A child who is ugly becomes a great poet, showing that outward ugliness does not prevent later greatness.

L112.10.p: The hero has only one arm and still performs heroic feats.

L112.11.p: The heroine is born with a pigeon's head instead of a human one, yet she goes on to become the central figure of the tale.

L113.p: The hero or heroine has a lowly or unpromising job or occupation, such as a servant or herdsman, yet still achieves great things.

L113.3.p: A poor weaver, a person who makes cloth on a loom, is the hero of the tale.

L113.4.p: A peasant, a poor rural farm worker, is the hero of the tale.

L113.6.p: A blacksmith, a metal worker who forges tools, is the hero of the tale.

L113.7.p: A quack doctor, an unqualified or fraudulent healer, is the hero of the tale.

L113.8.p: A barber rises to become king.

L113.9.p: A tailor, a person who sews clothes, is the hero of the tale.

L113.10.p: A flute player, a musician who plays the flute, is the hero of the tale.

L114.2.p: The hero is a spendthrift who wastes money freely.

L114.4.p: The hero is a cheat or trickster who succeeds through cheating.

L114.5.p: The hero has disgusting or repulsive habits.

L115.p: A foolish son, whom everyone expects to fail, nonetheless succeeds in the end.

L116.p: The hero or heroine is insane or mentally disturbed, yet still ends up succeeding.

L161.3.p: A mercenary soldier, or an exile, is accepted as the lover of a princess.

L175.p: A humble hero who has succeeded invites the king to his home and humbles him.

L175.1.p: A humble, lowly soldier who turns out successful gets a general or king to visit him, and then humbles that high-ranking person.

L176.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 327f. nn. 185f. (many references), (Zuñi): *Benedict II 336.
L176.p: A boy who is looked down on and despised wins a race against others.

L177.p: A boy who is looked down on and despised wins a gambling game.

L211.p: A choice must be made among objects hidden in caskets or similar containers; the plainest-looking casket holds the best prize.

L212.r: *Fb “hest” I 598b; Child II 444f., 450, 453f.; German: Grimm No. 57; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 62, 64; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 341, (Arikara): Dorsey CI XVII No. 16; West Indies: Flowers 559.
L212.p: Someone is offered a choice among several gifts, such as horses or armor, and the worst-looking one proves to be the best.

L212.1.p: A saint, offered any gift by God, chooses wisdom (and sometimes virginity) rather than something showier.

L212.2.p: Solomon, offered any gift by God, chooses wisdom, and is granted both wisdom and wealth.

L212.3.p: A hero is offered a choice between a long life and fame, and chooses fame.

L212.3.1.p: The hero states that fame or honor lasts longer than life itself.

L212.4.p: A girl offered five villages instead chooses a single modest privilege: to have light in her house on one night and to keep all animals that enter it, and then all kinds of livestock come to her.

L213.r: Treasure follows. Chauvin III 103 No. 13; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
L213.p: A poor girl is chosen over rich women, showing that the modest candidate is the best choice.

L213.1.p: A man chooses a wife from a crowd of women, picking the only poorly dressed one.

L213.2.p: A man chooses the ugliest girl as his bride.

L214.p: The old thing is chosen over the new one, and the old one turns out to be better.

L215.r: Hero refuses to take one that cries out “take me!” Roberts 204; Tonga: Beckwith Myth 25, Gifford 20; Africa (Benga): Nassau 114 No. 11; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 269 No. 81.
L215.p: An unpromising-looking magic object is chosen, and it turns out to be the valuable one.

L216.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 83.
L216.p: A poor-looking game or prize turns out to be rich and valuable.

L217.p: A man returns home to find his cottage replaced by a palace, and recognizes his wife only when she takes off her jewels and stands before him in her old rags; she prefers her familiar poverty to the new wealth.

L217.1.p: A weaver mourns the loss of his water vessel; offered many new riches, he prefers his old modest life.

L220.r: *Cox 480; *BP II 232; *MacCulloch Childhood 191; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 276 n. 18a.
L220.p: A character is rewarded because they make a modest request rather than a greedy one.

L221.r: *Type 425; *Fb “rose” III 80a, “guldæble” I 515b, “guldrok” I 514b; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 206b; Tegethoff 11; Italian Basile Pentamerone II No. 8; India: Thompson-Balys.
L221.p: When asked what gift she wants from her father's journey, the heroine humbly asks for something small, such as a flower, which later proves to be more than an ordinary gift, like a golden cloak or golden apple.

L221.1.p: The gift brought back from a journey is whatever the traveler first sees on returning home.

L222.r: *Köhler-Bolte I 188; BP I 214 n. 1; Gunkel Das Märchen im alten Testament (Tübingen, 1921) 100f.; Campbell Tales I 220 No. 13; Lang English Fairy Tales 136 No. 23; Gipsy: Aichele Zigeunermärchen 289 No. 69; Jewish: Neuman; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 110, 122.
L222.p: A small parting gift accompanied by a blessing is chosen over a large gift that comes with a parent's curse.

L222.1.r: Counsels chosen. Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 100, 304.
L222.1.p: On departure, the character chooses a modest parting gift of either money or advice, and the modest choice turns out better.

L222.2.p: On parting, the character chooses bones over meat as a gift, since bones thrown to pursuing dogs delay them and let the character escape.

L222.3.p: When offered money as a parting gift, a man chooses a magic stick instead, and the stick proves useful.

L222.4.p: When offered a parting gift, a character chooses a magic iron measure, which proves more valuable than the alternatives.

L225.r: *Types 300, 303; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; Icelandic: Boberg.
L225.p: A hero turns down a reward and rides away without taking it.

L250.p: A character who asks for only a modest share or plans modestly is rewarded more than one who asks for more.

L251.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 607; *Crane Vitry 168 No. 77; Alphabet No. 607.
L251.p: A beggar with a small bag receives more than a beggar with a large bag, because the large-bag beggar refuses small donations and so receives nothing.

L290.p: Miscellaneous tales in which modesty in business or conduct is rewarded.

L291.p: A king asks a prince whether he knows the secret of lasting prosperity or only prosperity for a day. The prince claims lasting prosperity and is captured; his wife, asked the same question, answers for a day and is honored.

L300.r: Chauvin II 204 No. 59; Irish myth: Cross.
L300.p: The weak or humble defeat the powerful or mighty, reversing the expected outcome.

L301.r: Wienert FFC LVI 35; Halm Aesop No. 150.
L301.p: The god Hermes gives everyone the same amount of wit, so the small people end up cleverer than the large ones.

L310.p: In a conflict the weaker side overcomes the stronger one.

L311.r: *Type 328; A. Stender-Petersen Acta Jutlandica VI (1934) 166ff.; Irish myth: Cross; English: Child II 35ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Japanese: Anesaki 311; Jewish: Neuman, I Samuel 17:23 (David and Goliath); N. A. Indian (Southern Paiute, Shivwits): Lowie JAFL XXXVII 150 No. 17; Guatamala Indian (Quiche): Alexander Lat. Am. 168ff.; Tuamotu: Beckwith Myth 476.
L311.p: A small or weak hero defeats a large fighter.

L311.1.p: A sick or ailing hero defeats his antagonist.

L311.2.p: A poorly armed hero defeats a well-armed opponent through strategy rather than strength.

L311.3.p: A poor prince defeats a king.

L311.4.p: A very small girl, who looks harmless, manages to drive a giant out of the country. The weak person wins against a far stronger opponent.

L311.5.p: A small boy defeats a gorilla that is in a furious rage. The little hero overcomes a huge, angry beast.

L312.p: A small but strong man beats a giant in a race. The underdog wins a contest of speed against a much larger opponent.

L315.p: A small animal defeats a much larger animal. The weak creature wins through cleverness or persistence.

L315.1.r: *Type 228; *BP II 437; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list No. 115.
L315.1.p: A bird flies into a large animal's ear and kills it. A tiny bird's entry into the ear proves fatal to the big beast.

L315.1.1.p: A mouse runs into a buffalo's ear and overcomes it. The small mouse defeats the much bigger buffalo by getting inside its ear.

L315.2.p: A mouse torments a bull, which cannot catch it. The small mouse keeps teasing the bull while staying out of its reach.

L315.3.p: A fox sets fire to a tree where an eagle has its nest, as revenge for the eagle stealing its cub. The weaker fox takes revenge on the stronger eagle.

L315.4.p: A mother ape sets fire to a bear, as revenge for the bear stealing her young. The ape takes revenge on the bear for taking her offspring.

L315.5.r: Chauvin II 81 No. 1; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 771; Japanese: Ikeda.
L315.5.p: A lark causes an elephant to fall over a cliff. The small bird brings down the huge elephant.

L315.5.1.p: A mouse kills an elephant by running up its trunk to its head and smearing poison over its brain. The tiny mouse uses poison to slay the huge elephant after the lark's trick.

L315.6.r: Wienert FFC LVI *48 (ET 76), 120 (ST 301); Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 187, 209; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 132, 137.
L315.6.p: Insects bite and pester a large animal until it is driven to despair or death. Many tiny insects wear down a giant creature.

L315.7.r: Wienert FFC LVI *51 (ET 106), 77 (ET 432), 113 (ST 237), 114 (ST 249); Halm Aesop No. 7.
L315.7.p: A dung beetle keeps destroying an eagle's eggs. The eagle finally lays its eggs in Zeus's lap, and the beetle makes Zeus shake his apron so the eggs break.

L315.8.p: A fish pricks a monster with its fins and defeats it. The small fish overcomes the huge monster by stabbing it.

L315.9.p: A falcon repeatedly attacks an eagle and defeats it. The smaller falcon wears the larger eagle down through persistent assault.

L315.10.p: Mice overcome a camel. Many small mice defeat a large camel.

L315.11.p: A lizard defeats a leopard. The small lizard beats the big cat.

L315.12.p: A rabbit slays a rhinoceros. The small rabbit kills the huge rhino.

L315.13.p: A hedgehog defeats a tiger by jumping into the tiger's mouth and tormenting it. The small hedgehog wins by getting inside the tiger and harassing it.

L315.14.p: Ants overcome a serpent. Many tiny ants defeat a snake.

L315.15.p: A small animal tricks a larger one into walking into a trap, so the weak creature wins.

L316.p: Rats, angered by the king, gnaw through the girths of his horses' saddles, so he loses the battle.

L318.p: Mice defeat woodcutters in a war, overcoming much larger human enemies.

L330.p: Small or weak creatures easily escape from danger that would catch larger ones.

L331.r: *Type 253; *BP III 355; Wienert FFC LVI 66 (ET 299), 113 (ST 240); Halm Aesop No. 26.
L331.p: Small fish slip through a net and get away while the large fish are caught.

L332.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 65), *113 (ST 241); Halm Aesop No. 291.
L332.p: Mice flee into their holes, where weasels cannot follow them.

L333.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 290; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 254*.
L333.p: A hummingbird sees a fowler's net that the boastful eagle fails to notice, and the eagle is trapped despite claiming sharp eyesight.

L350.p: Gentleness and mildness defeat violence and force.

L350.1.p: A queen advises her husband to win over his enemies with kindness, which succeeds where war had failed.

L350.2.p: A saint answers a pagan priest who has just struck a Christian with gentle words, and the priest is moved to repent.

L351.r: Wienert FFC LVI 43 (ET 7), 80 (ET 457), 136 (ST 419); Halm Aesop No. 82; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3900; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 381ff.; Russian: Andrejev No. 298*; Indonesia: DeVries’s list Nos. 95, 140. Cf. Halm No. 414.
L351.p: Sun and wind compete to make a traveler take off his coat: the sun's warmth succeeds, while the wind's blowing only makes him hold it tighter.

L351.1.p: In a version of the wind and sun contest, rain is the opponent and tries the same thing as the wind without success.

L351.2.p: People curse the sun for its burning rays and the wind for its hot breath, but bless the moon for its soft, cool, beautiful light.

L353.p: A gentle brother outlives his warlike brother and inherits the property.

L361.r: Scala Celi 48a No. 272; Alphabet No. 183; Herbert III 505, 570; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
L361.p: A priest who gives gentle penances succeeds where other priests with harsher ones fail.

L363.p: A goldsmith who has cheated everyone and has no friends gives money to a man who calls him friend.

L390.p: A miscellaneous group of tales in which the weak triumph over the strong in ways not covered by other headings.

L391.p: A tiny needle slips into an elk's stomach and kills it.

L391.1.p: A reed pricks a dog that urinates on it, driving the dog away.

L392.r: *DeCock Volkssage 31ff.; BP I 148 n. 2; Wesselski Mönchslatein 82 No. 75; Chauvin II 97 No. 55; Archiv f. d. Studium d. neueren Sprachen LXXXI 265; Germania II 481; Basset RTP VII 394ff.; Basset Contes Berbères 95f; *Bødker Exempler 297 No. 60.—Spanish: Keller, Espinosa III Nos. 275—277; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
L392.p: A mouse proves stronger than a wall, the wind, and a mountain.

L392.1.p: A tiny mosquito stings a proud king and shows it is stronger than a man who cannot escape it, so the weak overcome the mighty.

L393.p: A bride asks suitors what they can offer her, and a poor youth who has nothing but his love wins her.

L394.p: A slow-flying swan outlasts a fast crow in a flying contest, so speed is not what counts in the end.

L395.p: A frog, a tortoise and a fish each say how long they expect to live; only the frog, who expects a shorter life, escapes the fisherman's net.

L400.p: A proud person is brought down and loses their high position or good fortune.

L410.p: A proud ruler or god is humbled and brought down from power.

L410.1.p: A proud king is humbled and comes to realize that his pomp, wealth and power will not last.

L410.2.p: A king is defeated in battle and must flee without any money.

L410.3.p: A boastful king is insulted when a crow drops filth on him.

L410.4.p: A defeated king must become a peddler or a beggar to survive.

L410.5.p: A king is overthrown and made into a servant.

L410.6.p: A ruler is taken and held as a slave.

L410.7.p: A queen is forced to become a courtesan, a prostitute serving the powerful.

L411.r: *Type 757; **Varnhagen Ein indisches Märchen auf seine Wanderung durch die asiatischen und europäischen Literaturen (Berlin, 1882); Chauvin II 161 No. 51; *Wesselski Märchen 237 No. 49; Hibbard 58ff.; *Herbert III 202; *Oesterley No. 59; *Andraea Anglia Beiblatt XIII 302; *von der Hagen III cxv; bin Gorion Born Judas III 47ff., 299f.; *Goebel Jüdische Motive im Märchenhafte Erzählungsgut (Gleiwitz, 1932) 89ff.—Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
L411.p: While a proud king is in the bath or out hunting, an angel takes his form and place; the king is turned away everywhere until he repents of his arrogance.

L412.r: Type 836; Irish: Beal XXI 336, O’Suilleabhain 122; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 249; India: Thompson-Balys.
L412.p: A rich man who boasts that God cannot make him poor is made poor: while he is at church his property burns, and he returns home penniless.

L412.1.r: Ring is found in fish: she becomes poor. W. Jones Finger-Ring Lore (London, 1898) 440; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 19 No. 178.
L412.1.p: A woman throws a ring into the sea, boasting that she could no more become poor than the ring could be found again.

L413.r: *Chauvin V 33 No. 16; Spanish Exempla: Keller. Cf. Shelley’s “Ozymandias”.
L413.p: Only proud inscriptions remain to show that a once powerful king existed.

L414.p: A king vainly orders the tide to stop rising.

L414.1.p: A king vainly tries to measure the height of the sky and the depth of the sea.

L415.p: God punishes King David for pride in the size of his population by sending an angel to kill his people, and the punishment stops only when David repents.

L416.p: A proud king is forced to carry his enemy's shoes on his shoulders as a public sign that he has been defeated and must submit.

L416.1.p: A proud king is brought low when enemies take him prisoner.

L417.r: Wienert FFC LVI 80 (ET 455), 94 (ST 77); Halm Aesop No. 137.
L417.p: A god goes to a statue shop to sell his own statue and is dismayed to find it is priced lower than the statues of other gods.

L418.p: A proud king tries many schemes to keep a stolen treasure, but a servant of God recovers it, showing the king is weaker than God.

L419.p: A miscellaneous group of tales in which a proud ruler, who may be a god, is humbled.

L419.1.p: A goose boasts that it is better than a mushroom, but both are served up at the same meal, mocking its pride.

L419.2.p: A king or prince falls from power and ends up as a beggar.

L420.p: A person who reaches too high with ambition is punished for it.

L420.0.1.p: A man sets himself up as a god and is punished for this overweening ambition.

L421.p: A man tries to fly to heaven in a car supported by eagles and is punished for the attempt.

L421.1.p: A person tries to climb up to heaven and is punished for the attempt.

L423.r: A girl takes her goat to pasture and leaves him: “My God care for you!” Peter must run everywhere after the goat. *Dh II 188.
L423.p: Peter is allowed to act as God for a day, but he soon grows tired of the bargain and wants to give it up.

L424.p: A man who has never known unhappiness or want is swallowed up by the earth together with his whole household.

L425.p: A dream or prophecy that foretells future greatness leads to the dreamer being banished or imprisoned.

L427.p: A poor man who aspires to high office is made a cook instead.

L430.p: Someone who behaves arrogantly is paid back in kind.

L431.r: *Type 900; *BP I 443ff.; **Philippson König Drosselbart FFC L; Krappe Études ital. II 141ff.; *Gigas “Et eventyrs vandring” Litteratur og Historie (København, 1902); *Fb “bejler” IV 31b; Icelandic: Boberg; West Indies: Flowers 560.
L431.p: A haughty mistress is paid back in kind by her lover for her arrogant treatment of him.

L431.1.r: (Glove and the Lion.) *Shearin MLN XXVI 113; *Buchanan Modern Language Review IV 183 n. 1; Krappe MLN XXXIV 16; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 349 n. 256.
L431.1.p: A haughty mistress makes extravagant demands of her lover, and she is repaid for them.

L431.2.r: Boccaccio Decameron VIII No. 10 (Lee 266); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
L431.2.p: A scorned lover pretends to be a rich man and cheats his scornful mistress.

L431.3.p: A sneering princess becomes pregnant through magic, as a punishment for her scorn.

L432.r: *Chauvin II 174 No. 16, VIII 180 No. 212; *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 263 N. 232; *Basset 1001 Contes II 305.
L432.p: A once-proud man falls into poverty and must beg from the new husband of the woman he once rejected or wronged.

L432.1.p: Cruel brothers fall into poverty and have to beg charity from the sister they had abused.

L432.2.p: A poor father, whom the daughter he had banished does not recognize at first, begs from her and is finally recognized.

L432.2.1.p: A poor father begs from his prosperous daughter, whom he had forced to marry a poor man.

L432.3.p: A poor husband begs from the wife he had earlier driven away.

L432.4.p: The youngest brother, now poor, goes to his elder brothers looking for work.

L434.r: Icelandic: Hrafnkels saga Freysgods ch. 2ff. (ed. F. S. Cawley) (Cambridge, Mass., 1932).
L434.p: A proud farmer forbids anyone to ride his valuable horse without his permission. When a man rides it anyway, the farmer kills him, but as revenge the dead man's kin strip the farmer of most of his property.

L435.p: A self-righteous person is punished for their smugness or judgmental attitude.

L435.1.r: *Types 756A, 756B; BP III 463ff.; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 160ff., 250ff.; Wesselski Mönchslatein 21 No. 16; Alphabet No. 206; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 99, Beal XXI 332; Spanish: Espinosa II Nos 79f.
L435.1.p: A self-righteous hermit must do penance after saying that a condemned man deserves his punishment.

L435.1.1.r: Abbot tells him to search his own heart to see if he is free of sin before attacking others. Spanish Exempla: Keller.
L435.1.1.p: A self-righteous monk is rebuked by his abbot for his judgmental attitude.

L435.2.p: A self-righteous woman is punished for passing judgment on a girl who has had an illegitimate child.

L435.2.1.r: *Taylor Notes and Queries No. 251 (Feb., 1923) 96; *K. Nyrop Grevinden med de 365 Born (København, 1909); Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 469; Child II 67f., IV 463b.; *Köhler Lais der Marie de France@2 xc; *DeCock Volkssage 9ff.
L435.2.1.p: A woman is punished by being given 365 children, as penalty for condemning an unchaste girl.

L435.3.r: *Type 800; BP I 342; Wesselski Bebel I 126 No. 19.
L435.3.p: A self-righteous tailor who has reached heaven is expelled for hurling God's footstool at an old woman thief he saw on earth.

L435.4.p: A beggar takes the place of Christ on the cross, but is made to leave it because he grows impatient with the sinners.

L450.p: A proud animal ends up worse off than a humble one.

L451.p: A wild animal finds freedom more valuable than the comfortable life of a tame animal.

L451.1.r: He is shot. Type 245; Japanese: Ikeda.
L451.1.p: A tame bird and a wild bird talk, and the tame bird advises the wild one to look around him, meaning to see how well off he is.

L451.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 59 (ST 198), 124 (ST 328); Halm Aesop No. 321.
L451.2.p: A wild ass envies a tame ass until he sees how heavy the tame ass's burdens are.

L451.3.r: *Type 201; Crane Vitry 221 No. 217; Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 238), 124 (ST 326); Halm Aesop No. 278; Jacobs Aesop 206 No. 28; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 433; Scala Celi 76b No. 435; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
L451.3.p: A wolf chooses freedom and hunger over a dog's servitude and plenty.

L451.4.p: A parrot prefers a cold, wet nest in freedom to a life of luxury in a royal palace.

L452.p: A donkey envies a horse, thinking the horse has the better life, until he finds out the horse's life is harder or more dangerous than his own.

L452.1.p: A donkey envies a horse, but later sees the horse working hard turning a mill, and so stops envying him.

L452.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 58 (ET 191), 124 (ST 327); Halm Aesop No. 328; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
L452.2.p: A donkey envies a war-horse until he sees the horse wounded in battle, and then he no longer envies him.

L453.p: Of two mules, one carrying grain escapes danger while the one carrying gold is robbed, so the richer load brings the mule trouble.

L455.r: Later see their error. Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 169), 94 (ST 75).
L455.p: Lean dogs envy a fat dog kept in the arena, wishing they had his plumpness, not realizing his fatness comes with a worse fate.

L456.r: Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 230), 57 (ET 185), *92 (ST 44), 124 (ST 331); Halm Aesop No. 113.
L456.p: A calf pities a draft ox because the ox works hard, then the calf is taken to be slaughtered while the ox is spared.

L460.p: Miscellaneous tales in which a proud person or creature is brought low and suffers a reversal of fortune.

L461.r: *Type 77; Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 285), 140 (ST 465); Halm Aesop No. 128; *Crane Vitry 254 No. 274; Herbert III 23; Jacobs Aesop 206 No. 25.
L461.p: A stag scorns his slender legs and admires his antlers, but his antlers catch in the trees and trap him, while his legs would have saved him.

L462.p: A bird boasts about how warm its nest is, and a fox then destroys the nest.

L465.r: When well fed says, “My mother was a thoroughbred horse.” Later, hard worked, says, “My father was a miserable ass.” Wienert FFC LVI 64 (ET 275), 94 (ST 80); Halm Aesop No. 157.
L465.p: A mule boasts of its noble ancestry on both sides, but is humbled by being reminded that its parents were a donkey and a horse, so it is only a mixed-breed animal.

L471.p: A man scorns a storm and defies it, and the storm kills him.

L472.p: Zeus strikes down the giant Capaneus with a thunderbolt while he is climbing a ladder to attack the city.

L473.p: A proud or wealthy man is brought low through the actions of the gods.

L475.r: Wienert FFC LVI 75 (ET 409), 93 (ST 64); Halm Aesop No. 285.
L475.p: An oil lamp blown out by the wind, having believed it outshone the stars, is extinguished.

L476.p: A jackal sings boastfully about his deeds, falls from a tree, and is eaten by an alligator.

L478.r: Wienert FFC LVI 48 (ET 75), 92 (ST 57); Halm Aesop No. 234.
L478.p: Gnats defeat a lion, but are then killed in turn by a spider.

L482.p: When men become too prosperous or happy, the gods make their lives more difficult.

L482.1.p: Because men are too rich, greedy gods create beings to make them poor.

L482.1.1.p: Because men are too rich, gold is sent below the ground, out of their reach.

L482.2.p: Because men are too rich, weeds are created to ruin their harvests.

L482.3.p: Because people have become too proud, the creator makes snakes to bring them down. This is a reversal where good fortune leads to trouble.

L482.4.p: Because people have become too fearless, a tiger is created to frighten them. Excess confidence is cut down by a dangerous animal.

L482.5.p: Because people enjoy themselves too much, a disease is created to make their lives harder. Too much happiness is answered with sickness.
